Description
Osprey Wilds Environmental Learning Center is a public, non-profit residential learning center on Grindstone Lake near Sandstone, MN that provides outdoor educational opportunities to diverse audiences in an intimate setting.

Residential and day-use environmental education  experiences for thousands of K-12 students from across the Midwest focus on a selection of adventure, team building, outdoor/environmental education, cultural, natural history and science, wildlife ecology, and renewable energy classes. We are accredited by Cognia, and have over 50 years of environmental education experience and an incredible variety of programs and audiences. 

Working at Osprey Wilds as a Fellow is a one-of-a-kind opportunity! Join our team and gain experience in current environmental education methods, as well as knowledge of Minnesota’s unique biomes and natural history through training seminars, direct mentorship, graduate level coursework, and on-the-job learning.

Key Responsibilities
Teach ecology, wildlife, adventure, and cultural classes to large and small groups of all ages, including evening and weekend programming.
Serve as the primary representative and host to visiting conference and retreat groups (includes being on-call for overnight visitors and serving food).
Plan and lead summer camp programming and free-time activities.
Attend weekly staff meetings and regular training throughout the year.
Provide basic husbandry for Osprey Wilds Animal Ambassadors, including raptors, corvids, mammals, invertebrates and herps.
Complete other self-directed projects or projects/tasks as assigned. 

Benefits
Compensation includes a $275/week stipend
Delicious, healthy meals during the week (when groups are present) made from locally sourced ingredients and produce from our Trapp Farm
Private room in staff housing adjacent to Grindstone Lake
Four days off per two-week pay period, 13 PTO days, accrual of up to 80 hours of paid sick leave
Access to an Employee Assistance Program
Employee discounts for events and lodging for family members and in the Osprey Wilds store

To Apply
Please send a resume, cover letter, and three references to Amy Heusinkvelt at [email removed].

Graduate student openings in organismal biology or physiological ecology at the University of Florida
  The Gillooly Lab in the Department of Biology at the University of Florida has openings for 1-2 graduate students beginning in Fall 2027. Research in the lab is diverse but generally falls under the category of comparative organismal biology or physiological ecology. Lab members use a variety of approaches, including mathematical modeling, experimentation and field studies. Description
The Chattopadhyay Hydroecology Lab, led by Dr. Somsubhra Chattopadhyay at Texas State University, is recruiting a PhD student in environmental hydrology to start in August 2027. Funding is available for 4.5 years.

Texas rivers are changing fast: floods are getting flashier, droughts longer, and streams that once flowed year-round now go dry. The student will help work out what that means for the rivers and the life in them, combining ecohydrologic modelling and fieldwork in the Texas Hill Country. The project can grow in one of three directions:

Rivers on the edge of drying. When, where and why do Hill Country streams stop flowing, and what happens to connectivity and aquatic life when they do?
Forecasting rivers in a hotter, thirstier Texas. Use SWAT+ and data-driven models to project how climate, land use and water demand will reshape floods, low flows and environmental flows.
Linking flow to life. Pair hydrology with environmental DNA and field biodiversity data to find the flow conditions that keep rivers diverse and functioning.
The student will shape the final direction together with Dr. Chattopadhyay and will also lead one chapter that uses large-scale existing data or synthesizes existing research.

Applicants should have a background in hydrology, water resources engineering, environmental science, earth sciences, ecology or a related field. Experience with hydrologic modeling, GIS, R, Python or statistics is desirable. Strong quantitative skills and an interest in interdisciplinary research are especially welcome.

The student will be expected to mentor undergraduate researchers, be a collaborative member of the research group, and take part in Biology Department activities. The student will serve as a teaching assistant for 4 semesters. Applicants from all backgrounds are encouraged to apply, and international applicants are welcome. The degree is a PhD in Integrative and Applied Biology.

To apply: Complete the online application form by November 30, 2026: https://forms.gle/Pwr1TUGtZWYrvX5DA
The form asks for your CV, short answers about your interests and experience, and contact details for two references. Applications are accepted only through the form. Shortlisted applicants will be interviewed in December, and the selected candidate will then apply to the Texas State Graduate College by its February 1, 2027 deadline.

More about the lab: https://schatteco.github.io/chattopadhyayhydroecologylab/join.html

Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis and applications may close before the deadline.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in St. Paul, Minnesota..

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: Fusarium Head Blight is one of the most devastating diseases of wheat, barley, and other cereal crops and is a persistent threat to U.S. agriculture, causing economic losses exceeding $1B in epidemic years. This opportunity investigates how Fusarium causes disease by interacting with its hosts and how it produces harmful mycotoxins that accumulate in cereal grains during infection. Alongside your mentor, you will design experiments, collect and analyze data, and collaborate with lab members to achieve project goals. The project will enable new strategies for controlling this disease and reducing mycotoxins in the food supply, which will increase the value of cereal crops grown by U.S. farmers and enhance overall U.S. Food Security and U.S. Food Safety.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will gain experience in molecular biology, protein biochemistry, plant/fungal genetics, and bioinformatics, as well as collaboration skills.

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is J. Mitch Elmore ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: January 2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is part time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing a doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields.

Description
Join an interdisciplinary team that includes researchers in plant ecology, remote sensing, and computer science as part of a collaboration between the USDA Agricultural Research Service and Boise State University. The successful candidate will contribute to an existing deep learning pipeline to classify rangeland plant species in unoccupied aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery and apply that dataset to research questions ranging from plant community ecology, invasive species detection, pollinator floral resources, restoration outcomes, and/or wildfire burn severity.

This fellowship is part of ARS’s SCINet/Artificial Intelligence (AI) Center of Excellence Research Participation Program and offers research opportunities to motivated postdoctoral fellows interested in solving agriculture-related problems at a range of spatial and temporal scales. The objective of these fellowships is to facilitate cross-disciplinary, cross-location research through collaborative research on problems of interest to each applicant and amenable to or requiring HPC resources. ·         Strong programming skills in R or Python

·         Background in dryland, rangeland, or plant ecology
·         Experience publishing in peer-reviewed journals
·         Strong written and verbal communication skills

Preferred Qualifications:

·         Familiarity with deep learning and/or machine learning

Applicants are not expected to have expertise in every area. We encourage candidates with strong ecological backgrounds who are excited about developing their deep learning and artificial intelligence/machine learning skills.

Description

Position Title: Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship – Optimizing Invasive Cattail Treatment Effectiveness for Native Vegetation, Waterfowl, and Marsh Birds in Prairie Wetlands

Location: Grand Forks, ND, with field work in western MN (Otter Tail, Pope, Stevens, Traverse, Big Stone, Swift, Chippewa, and Todd counties)

Start Date: Spring 2027 for fieldwork with the potential of a January or August 2027 official grad program start

Position Description: We are seeking a PhD student with broad interest in wetland habitat management and wetland biology/ecology (especially wetland plant, waterfowl, and marsh bird communities) to join a research team comparing the effectiveness and longevity of several treatments for invasive cattail in seasonal prairie pothole wetlands, with the goal of informing habitat management techniques for waterfowl and marsh birds. 

Invasive cattail species (Typha angustifolia, T. x glauca) have dramatically proliferated across North America’s prairie pothole region since the mid-twentieth century. Unlike native cattail, invasive cattail forms thick monocultures, impacting native plant diversity, displacing wildlife food plants, and disrupting habitat structure. The overarching research project is a before-after/control-impact study comparing the outcomes of four cattail treatment methods across approximately 50 wetlands in western Minnesota for the first 3 years following treatment. The selected candidate will collect and analyze post-treatment data, including (1) vegetation type and structure data from vegetation surveys and high-resolution aerial imagery from an uncrewed aerial system (UAS; i.e., a drone), (2) waterfowl and secretive marsh bird abundance from UAS surveys, and (3) waterfowl and secretive marsh bird occupancy from passive acoustic recording units. The selected candidate will analyze these data streams toward the goal of producing practical information for land managers to balance frequency of needed retreatment versus cost per treatment. The candidate will also participate in sharing results with natural resource managers and the public. Given the vast amount of data collected, there is the potential to develop additional questions of interest to the candidate.     

This research is highly collaborative, offering opportunity to engage with professionals in various career tracks and agencies/entities. Partners include scientists and wetland managers from the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Delta Waterfowl, and the University of Minnesota. Good communication skills will be key to success in this collaborative team.  

This research will have a heavy field travel component, with the PhD student stationed full-time in the field from April to August in 2027, 2028, and possibly 2029. During this time, the student will lead field technicians in data collection. Co-PIs will provide close support, including regular in-person presence. Field work will include piloting UAS’s, driving 4WD trucks and UTVs, hiking across prairie, and wading/collecting data in shallow wetlands with thick emergent vegetation, in a variety of weather conditions (cold early spring to hot summer temperatures).  

Minimum qualifications
·        Master’s degree in plant ecology, wildlife biology, biology, ecology, or a related field
·        Commitment to fostering an inclusive and respectful work environment
·        Strong communication and collaboration skills for working within a large research team
·        Interest in research spanning all project lines of inquiry (wetland management techniques, wetland plant biology/ecology, avian biology/ecology, wetland soils), and research experience pertinent to 1-2 of those topics
·        Willingness to work full-time in the field April-August (with field lodging provided by University of North Dakota)
·        Field work experience relevant to at least one of the project data collection methods
·        Already possess or willing to obtain (with guidance from PIs) a FAA Part 107 license (Remote Pilot Certificate) for operating UAS
·        Experience with statistical analysis of biological data and analysis software (e.g., R)
·        Experience with GIS software (e.g., ArcGIS) 
·        Strong writing skills
·        Experience prioritizing research project tasks and setting realistic timelines for completion

Preferred qualifications
·        Experience leading field crews in data collection
·        At least one peer-reviewed scientific publication
·        Research experience in multiple lines of project inquiry (wetland management techniques, wetland plant biology/ecology, avian biology/ecology, wetland soils) 
·        Field work experience with multiple project data collection methods (e.g., waterfowl surveys using UAS with thermal and EO sensors, plant surveys, passive acoustic recording units, creating orthomosaics from UAS imagery, wetland soil sampling) 

Salary and benefits: $30,240/year plus a tuition waiver. Student is expected to cover the modest student fees that are not an expense that can be covered by grants. The position is primarily funded through a research assistantship through June 2030. The selected candidate will be expected to work a teaching assistantship for 1-2 semesters to develop teaching/mentoring experience and to meet project budget constraints. 

To apply: Please e-mail a cover letter summarizing your interest and qualifications for the position, CV, and names and contact information of three professional references to Dr. Susan Ellis-Felege ([email removed]). For full consideration, please apply by November 15, 2026. Questions about the position may be addressed to Dr. Ellis-Felege ([email removed]) and/or Dr. Megan Fitzpatrick ([email removed])

Contact
Susan Felege
701-777-3699
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Piller are recruiting two highly motivated M.S. students to begin in Spring 2027 in the Department of Biological Sciences and Center for Environmental Research at Southeastern Louisiana University. Both positions are supported by a funded, interdisciplinary research project investigating blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) ecology, movement, population connectivity, and environmental health throughout the beautiful and unique Lake Pontchartrain Basin in coastal Louisiana. Each assistantship includes a 12-month stipend of $18,000 per year for two years and a full tuition waiver, with research support and opportunities for professional conference travel.

Location

The selected student will investigate blue crab population genetic structure and connectivity using molecular approaches. Research will involve genetic sampling, laboratory analyses, and bioinformatics to interpret molecular data and better understand population connectivity across the basin.
Both students will have opportunities to incorporate environmental chemistry, contaminant exposure, and histological analyses into their thesis research, depending on their interests. Students will receive training in research design, data analysis, and scientific communication, with opportunities to present findings at scientific conferences and publish in peer-reviewed journals.

Application deadline:  November 15, 2026 (or until filled) 
 Responsibilities:  I am seeking a MS student to help assess the status and guide recovery of the federally endangered Spruce Fir Moss Spider (SFMS) and its microhabitat in high elevation spruce-fir ecosystems of the southern Appalachians. Specifically, the student will leverage existing data to estimate the probability of SFMS occupancy across potentially suitable habitat units, use environmental logger data to investigate how spider microhabitats were impacted by Hurricane Helene, and design/implement surveys to assess and guide habitat restoration and recovery efforts in spruce-fir ecosystems. Responsibilities will include analyzing spider survey data collected under a long-term monitoring protocol, assisting with spider surveys in high elevation forests, deploying and maintaining environmental sensors/loggers, conducting geospatial and statistical analyses, developing databases, writing a MS proposal, thesis, and technical reports, and completing coursework pursuant to a MS degree. The selected candidate will be advised by Dr. Cathy Jachowski and will work with a wide range of collaborators from state and federal agencies, NGOs, and universities. 
  Project Description: Hurricane Helene caused widespread flooding, landslides, and destruction across the southern Appalachian region in September 2024. These impacts caused long-term and potentially permanent changes to terrestrial and aquatic habitat distribution, ecosystem structure, and function. Field evaluations and monitoring are required to understand how baseline ecological conditions changed following these large-scale, geological changes in terrestrial and aquatic habitats. Graduate students working on this project will be part of a dynamic and multi-disciplinary team at Clemson University with expertise across the fields of forestry, wildlife, fisheries, and fire ecology. Team members will work closely with federal, state, and non-governmental organizations to communicate findings and inform ongoing, on-the-ground restoration and recovery efforts aimed at focal species, ecosystems and important forest resources.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Mayaguez, Puerto Rico.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: This project aims to evaluate the susceptibility of different coffee varieties to coffee leaf rust (CLR) and to assess the potential of natural biocontrol agents (mycoparasites) against Hemileia vastatrix. You will gain experience preparing fungal growth media and using standard laboratory equipment such as autoclaves, sterilizers, centrifuges, and homogenizers. You will also learn to identify key symptoms and signs of CLR, and conduct disease surveys (assessing incidence and severity) across coffee fields in Puerto Rico.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn to evaluate coffee-variety susceptibility to coffee leaf rust (CLR) caused by Hemileia vastatrix.
Gain experience assessing natural fungal biocontrol agents, including mycoparasites, for their potential to suppress CLR.
Develop laboratory skills in preparing fungal media and operating standard equipment such as autoclaves, sterilizers, centrifuges, and homogenizers.
Learn to recognize CLR symptoms and signs and conduct field disease surveys measuring disease incidence and severity in Puerto Rican coffee farms.
Prepare H. vastatrix inoculum and conduct pathogenicity assays using spore suspensions on coffee plants and detached leaf tissues.
Build molecular-biology skills through DNA extraction, PCR amplification, and sequence analysis of CLR pathogens and associated mycoparasites.
Gain practical greenhouse and field-management experience, including coffee planting, fertilization, weed management, irrigation, and pesticide application under established protocols.
Strengthen experimental-design, plant-pathology, data-collection, and disease-management skills relevant to sustainable coffee production.
Through these activities, you will develop or strengthen practical skills in plant pathology, disease evaluation, and plant-pathogen interactions.

UNIVERSITY OF ALABAMA

DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY & THE ENVIRONMENT

Assistant Professor, Tenure Track

Position Summary
The Department of Geography & the Environment at the University of Alabama seeks an assistant professor (9-month, tenure track) broadly trained in Environmental Science, Earth Science, or Physical Geography.

Detailed Position Information
The Department of Geography & the Environment at the University of Alabama (https://geography.ua.edu/) seeks an assistant professor (9-month, tenure track) broadly trained in Environmental Science, Earth Science, or Physical Geography. The successful candidate will be expected to teach Introduction to Environmental Science (a large enrollment, natural lab science credit course) and develop courses in atmospheric, landscape, forest, and/or river systems designed to engage undergraduates in our Environmental Science and Geography degree programs through experiential-based learning. A Ph.D. in Environmental Science, Earth Science, Physical Geography, or a closely related field is required at the time of appointment.

Potential areas of expertise may include landscape ecology, soil, biogeography, geomorphology, conservation, biodiversity, natural resources, environmental pollution, climatology, water resources, and/or physical hydrology. While the position is open to a wide range of specialties, some integration of human-environmental interactions is preferred. Successful candidates will be expected to develop an externally funded research program that is nationally and internationally regarded within their area of expertise, while delivering high-quality, engaged teaching. 

About the Department of Geography & the Environment (GYE): Through the efforts of 28 total faculty members, the GYE Department offers undergraduate degrees in Environmental Science (BS), Geography (BA/BS), and graduate degrees in Geography (MS and PhD). Currently, there are ~200 undergraduate majors, and ~60 graduate students. Ranked in the top 15 Geography programs for research production by Academic Analytics, faculty research centers on three areas: Earth Systems and Environmental Science, Environment and Society, and Geographic Information Systems and Remote Sensing. The GYE Department is housed in two buildings (Bevill Energy Building and the Shelby Interdisciplinary Sciences Building), and these spaces include several wet labs and computational labs, as well as newly renovated offices and meeting spaces.

The Department of Geography and the Environment sits within the Barefield College of Arts & Sciences (BCAS). Eighty percent of the University of Alabama’s core curriculum is offered through BCAS. The College also houses several educational and research resources, including the Alabama Museum of Natural History and Moundville Archeological Park, the University of Alabama’s Arboretum, the J. Nicholene Bishop Biological Station, and the Center for Freshwater Studies, which offers aquatic chemistry services. BCAS supports faculty professional development through sabbaticals and pre-tenure leaves, as well.

UA is home to the Alabama Water Institute (AWI), which serves as a hub of water-focused research and education, for federal agencies co-located on the UA campus, including the NOAA National Water Center and the U.S. Geological Survey’s Hydrologic Instrumentation Facility, as well as being the home of the Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH), the Global Water Security Center, and CONSERVE. Numerous members of the Department of Geography and the Environment are affiliates of the Alabama Water Institute and conduct CIROH-funded research in continental to watershed scale hydrologic modeling, non-contact water observation, geospatial analyses, and social dimensions of water hazards. Three of the AWI’s key educational programs, the Water Prediction Innovators Summer Institute, the USGS FLOW Academy, and the NSF-funded National Science Traineeship Program: Water R2O are led by faculty in the Department of Geography and the Environment. In addition to providing exceptional professional training for our students, these programs offer graduate student and postdoctoral fellow recruitment opportunities for faculty at UA.

The state of Alabama is one of the most biologically and geomorphologically diverse landscapes in North America, and it is crossed by 17 major river basins. This makes the state an incredible living laboratory, teeming with outdoor exploration opportunities to observe wildlife and nature that includes mountain foothills, large tracts of forested lands, and expansive coastline, all within short drives of the UA campus. The city of Tuscaloosa is a vibrant, college town with daily Amtrak service to New Orleans, LA and Atlanta, GA.

Minimum Qualifications
A Ph.D. in Environmental Science, Earth Science, Physical Geography, or a closely related field is required at the time of appointment.

Instructions and Required Materials for Application
Applicants should complete the online application at https://careers.ua.edu/jobs/search/AS. The application must include: 1. A letter of application outlining your qualifications and interest in the position. 2. A current curriculum vita. 3. A research statement. 4. A teaching statement. 5. Contact information for three professional references. Review of applications will begin November 2026, and the search will continue until the position is filled. The expected start date of the position is August 16, 2027. Questions about the position can be directed to search committee chair, Professor Lisa Davis, [email removed].

Lisa Davis

Located in the vibrant community of http://www.wallawalla.org/, http://whitman.edu/ is home to an intellectually diverse, dynamic, and supportive community of some 500 staff and faculty serving roughly 1,500 students from the local region and across the globe. With exceptional students, accomplished faculty and staff, and engaged alumni, Whitman College continues to build on its national reputation for academic excellence as one of the top undergraduate, liberal arts colleges in the country.
The Department of Biology seeks applicants for a tenure-track position beginning August 2027, with expertise in ecology, at the rank of assistant professor. Applicants must have a Ph.D. at the start of the position.  
The standard annual teaching load is five courses, which will include some combination of lecture and/or lab courses in their area of expertise within ecology, non-majors environmental biology (and/or other courses that contribute to the College's general education requirements), introductory biology, and mentorship of students as they prepare their senior theses. The successful candidate will also offer research opportunities of interest to students in Biology.  This candidate will join a highly collaborative department that supports and engages our diverse and enthusiastic pool of life science majors. The Biology department provides ample opportunity for faculty to engage in field courses and the successful candidate will have the opportunity to work closely with the interdisciplinary Environmental Studies program. 
The College provides a generous pre-tenure sabbatical program and professional development support for both research and teaching. The successful candidate will demonstrate potential to sustain an active scholarly or creative research agenda and to participate in faculty governance, mentorship, or other forms of service in ways that fit their interests and talents. 
Whitman College is committed to fostering an inclusive learning community that values diverse identities, experiences, and perspectives. In the cover letter, candidates should describe their interest in teaching undergraduates, majors as well as non-majors, at all levels of instruction. In doing so, candidates should address how their classroom and scholarly practices will advance equity and inclusion in the learning environment. 
To apply, go to https://apply.interfolio.com/190454. References will only be contacted for applicants who reach the interview stage.
Review of applications will begin September 15th, 2026.
